facts.claim: "Built on Bones" is the opening title track of Emily Scott Robinson's six-song EP/song cycle for the Witches of Shakespeare's Macbeth. The EP was released October 28, 2022 on Oh Boy Records.
In the song cycle, the title track is the prophecy the Witches deliver. It foretells Macbeth's rise to power and his death.
Emily Scott Robinson wrote and composed all the songs. Brandy Zdan produced, Teddy Morgan engineered and mixed, and Richard Dodd mastered.
The EP was recorded at The Creative Workshop in Nashville. The Bandcamp page says the recording was made in May 2022.
Robinson sings and plays guitar. Alisa Amador and Lizzy Ross of Violet Bell sing as the three Witches in three-part harmony.

Other musicians on the record are Ellen Angelico (electric and baritone guitar), Josh Grange (pedal steel, piano, electric guitar), Aaron Haynes (drums), Vanessa McGowan and Teddy Morgan (bass), Eamon McLoughlin (fiddle), Kaitlyn Raitz (cello), and Kristin Weber (violin, string arrangements).

The songs were originally commissioned for Telluride Theatre's Macbeth. Robinson directed the music and played Hecate on stage. After a strong fan response she recorded them with Zdan, Amador and Ross.
Theatre director Colin Sullivan asked Robinson in spring 2021 to compose music for Macbeth. Their idea was to make the Witches beautiful, tempting, powerful and playful, instead of ugly and evil.
Robinson said the title track was the first song she wrote for the production. She had just finished writing American Siren.
Robinson said she, Ross, Amador and Zdan intended to heal the lineage of women who came before them and to declare that women's power and magic can't be controlled by a violent patriarchy.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Americana/folk singer-songwriter tradition on John Prine's Oh Boy Records, here applied to a theatrical, feminist retelling of Macbeth with Tom Waits-inspired production and southern gothic atmosphere.

draft:
The whole of **Built on Bones** rests on one word, sung three times over and over until it stops meaning anything and starts working like a spell. Between those repetitions, Emily Scott Robinson slips in the prophecy that Shakespeare's Witches hand to Macbeth: his rise, his fall, the forest that will walk. It opens her six-song cycle for the Witches, and it was the first song she wrote for the job, just after finishing *American Siren*.

The job came from Telluride Theatre. Director Colin Sullivan asked Robinson in spring 2021 to score his *Macbeth*, and the two agreed the Witches should be beautiful, tempting, powerful and playful rather than ugly and evil. You can hear that choice everywhere. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls out slow arpeggios, a cello (Kaitlyn Raitz plays on the record) holds long notes beneath it, and the tempo sways gently. Robinson's lead is clear and unhurried. Then Alisa Amador and Lizzy Ross of Violet Bell come in as the other two Witches, and the three-part harmony stacks tight and keeps thickening. Producer Brandy Zdan keeps the room intimate and clean, so nothing sounds like a cauldron. It sounds like a lullaby, which is the unsettling part.

The words aren't gentle at all. "Everything here is built on bones" is a historian's line as much as a witch's: every crown, every road, every kingdom stands on somebody's dead. "You cannot wash it white with snow" reaches ahead to Lady Macbeth scrubbing at her hands, guilt that no amount of cleaning will lift. And "A soldier not from woman born" is the riddle that will undo the king, delivered as calmly as a weather report.

That calm is where the feeling lives. These Witches aren't gloating. They warn, over and over. They tell Macbeth to hide his face, to seek to know no more tonight, that despair waits for him. There's pity in it, and something colder beside it: they know men will do what they've been told they'll do, and they sing it anyway. The two feelings never settle. Robinson said she, Ross, Amador and Zdan meant the record to heal the line of women who came before them, and to declare that women's power can't be controlled by a violent patriarchy. Heard that way, the bones belong to the women too. The harmony is three voices who've seen this story before and refuse to be its villains.

It ends with the word stripped down to "bones," the harmonies climbing into octaves, on John Prine's old label Oh Boy, a long way from Scotland and right at home.

You leave it hearing doom sung with tenderness, and you can't decide whether the Witches are cursing Macbeth or mourning him.

factCheck.claim: The song leans on one word, sung three times over and over, until it works like a spell
factCheck.note: The lyrics repeat 'Everything everything everything' after nearly every line. The body now names the word. The spell comparison is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: The song delivers the Witches' prophecy to Macbeth: his rise, his fall, the forest that will walk
factCheck.note: Researched facts say the title track is the prophecy that foretells Macbeth's rise and death. The lyrics mention Birnam Wood.

factCheck.claim: It opens her six-song cycle and was the first song she wrote for the job, just after finishing American Siren
factCheck.note: Both points are in the Bandcamp and Nashville Scene facts.

factCheck.claim: Telluride Theatre commissioned the music; director Colin Sullivan asked Robinson in spring 2021; the Witches were to be beautiful, tempting, powerful and playful rather than ugly and evil
factCheck.note: Matches the BrooklynVegan facts. 'Score his Macbeth' was reworded to 'compose music for Macbeth'.

factCheck.note: All three passes agree on the fingerpicked guitar. Passes 1 and 3 agree on the sustained cello.

factCheck.note: All passes say slow and gentle, flowing or swaying.

factCheck.claim: Robinson's lead is clear and unhurried
factCheck.note: 'Clear and direct' is backed by passes 1 and 3. 'Unhurried' was only loosely backed, so it was changed to 'direct'.

factCheck.claim: Amador and Ross of Violet Bell come in as the other two Witches; the three-part harmony stacks tight and keeps thickening
factCheck.note: Their roles and the three-part harmony are credited. Tight, stacked harmonies are backed by passes 2 and 3. 'Then... come in' and 'keeps thickening' describe order and arc within the clip, so they were removed.

factCheck.claim: Producer Brandy Zdan keeps the room intimate and clean
factCheck.note: Zdan is credited as producer. Intimate and clean are each backed by two passes.

factCheck.claim: 'Everything here is built on bones'; 'You cannot wash it white with snow'; 'A soldier not from woman born'
factCheck.note: All three quotes match the lyrics exactly.

factCheck.claim: The snow line reaches ahead to Lady Macbeth scrubbing at her hands
factCheck.note: Lady Macbeth and the handwashing scene are not in the evidence. Replaced with a reading of the line as blood that won't come clean.

factCheck.claim: The soldier line is the riddle that will undo the king, delivered as calmly as a weather report
factCheck.note: The lyrics say the soldier 'will come for you', and the prophecy foretells Macbeth's death. 'King' was dropped. Only pass 2 says 'calm', so the delivery description was softened to plain.

factCheck.claim: They tell Macbeth to hide his face, seek to know no more tonight, and that despair waits; men will do what they've been told
factCheck.note: A reading of the lyrics 'Hide your face from prophesy', 'Seek to know no more tonight', 'Despair you will upon the sight' and 'men will do as they're foretold'.

factCheck.claim: Robinson said she, Ross, Amador and Zdan meant to heal the line of women before them and declare women's power can't be controlled by a violent patriarchy

factCheck.note: The lyric structure shows the closing 'Bones / Bones' lines, and the lyrics mark octave harmonies. 'Harmonies climbing' was reworded as an ordering of the lyric structure, not a sound arc.
